lessons.title: Reading: The Life of Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ
lessons.notes_html:
The Story in Short

Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ is the last Rasool of Allah. He was born in Makkah Mukarramah in a tribe named Quraish. His father Hazrat Abdullah died before his birth, and his mother died when he was only six years old. His grandfather Hazrat Abdul Muttalib took care of him. When Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ reached the age of eight, his grandfather passed away, and he came under the guardianship of his uncle, Abu Talib.

Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ helped his uncle in his successful caravan business. He worked with honesty and truthfulness, and soon earned a good reputation in a short time.

Hazrat Khadija (RA) was the most respected lady of her time. She heard about Hazrat Muhammad's ﷺ reputation as being truthful, reliable and noble, so she entrusted him to take her caravan of goods to Syria and sell it. Her old and trusted slave Maysarah accompanied him during the tour. Maysarah was impressed by his integrity, strength of character, adherence to principles, amicable dealings and business abilities.

On the way back from Syria, Maysarah reported everything about Rasool's ﷺ honesty and intelligence to Hazrat Khadija (RA). She too was impressed by his nobility, and sent him a marriage proposal and became the first wife of Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ.

Rasoolullah ﷺ was immensely renowned for his integrity, and even his staunch enemies called him "Al Sadiq" (the truthful) and "Al Amin" (the trustworthy one).

The Letter to Heraclius

Once Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ wrote a letter to the Emperor of Byzantium, Heraclius, and invited him to embrace Islam. Upon reading the letter, the Emperor summoned Abu Sufyan to interrogate him about the Rasoolullah ﷺ. Abu Sufyan was one of the firmest opponents of Islam at that time. Despite that, he testified that the Rasoolullah ﷺ possessed exemplary qualities of honesty and trustworthiness and preached pure monotheism.

Justice and Kindness

Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ was also a loving father and a compassionate and merciful husband. He always showed respect towards women. Throughout his life, he always behaved well. Justice is another noble and magnificent characteristic of Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ. He always advised people to be just and kind.

Once a woman from Bani Makhzum committed theft. Due to her stature in the tribe, some prominent members came to Rasoolullah ﷺ and mediated on her behalf to save her from punishment. The Rasool ﷺ refused to forgive her crime due to her worldly status and expressed displeasure, saying: "Many a community ruined itself in the past as they only punished the poor and ignored the offences of the exalted." (Sahih al-Bukhari 3733)

Helping Others — The Dialogue

The unit's dialogue shows how we can help others in daily life. Dawood greets an old man and offers his help. The old man's shopping bag has torn open on the road side, and his fruit has scattered. Dawood brings a new bag in a few minutes and puts all the fruit in it. The old man thanks him and asks his name. Dawood says he likes to help others because Allah helps those who help others. The dialogue teaches that good deeds, like helping an old man on the road, are a part of our daily life.

Word Meanings

  • reliability — consistency
  • summoned — called
  • cloak — shawl
  • staunch — firmest

Key Points

  • Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ belonged to the tribe of Quraish, and he was born in Makkah Mukarramah.
  • After the death of his grandfather Hazrat Abdul Muttalib, he came under the guardianship of his uncle Abu Talib.
  • Maysarah reported to Hazrat Khadija (RA) that Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ was honest and intelligent, and that his integrity and business abilities had impressed everyone on the Syria tour.
  • Hazrat Khadija (RA) sent a marriage proposal to Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ because she was impressed by his nobility, honesty and truthfulness — the same qualities for which even his enemies called him Al Sadiq and Al Amin.
  • Abu Sufyan, though a firm opponent of Islam, testified before Heraclius that the Rasoolullah ﷺ was honest and trustworthy and preached pure monotheism.
  • The incident of the woman from Bani Makhzum shows his sense of justice and fairness: he refused to spare a rich and prominent woman from punishment, because justice is the same for the poor and the exalted.
  • The life of Rasoolullah ﷺ is a role model for us, and we can learn many things by following his code of conduct, which will make us successful in this world and the world hereafter.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: Compound Words and Homophones
lessons.notes_html:
Compound Words

A compound word is made by joining two words together; the joined words name one thing or one idea. In this unit we learn to recognise the compound words hidden inside sentences and to see the two words each one is made of.

  • fingernail — finger + nail. It names one thing, the nail on a finger, so it is written as a single word.
  • flashlight — flash + light. It is the small electric light of the mobile phone.
  • armchair — arm + chair. It is a comfortable chair with supports for the arms.
  • firefighters — fire + fighters. It names the people whose job is to put out fires.

Fill in the Blanks — The Book's Sentences Completed

  • I am not allowed to go to the market alone.
  • Who ate my pancakes?
  • The air fare of Turkey is very high.
  • Please move forward.
  • Can you please grate the cheese for me?

Homophones

The unit also teaches us to differentiate between homophones — words that sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: whether/weather, seen/scene, herd/heard, hare/hair, they're/there/their. Choosing the right spelling depends on the meaning of the sentence.

Key Points

  • A compound word joins two words into one word with one meaning, like fingernail, flashlight, armchair and firefighters.
  • Homophones sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning, so we must pick the word that fits the sense of the sentence.

lessons.title: Grammar: Types of Nouns
lessons.notes_html:
Kinds of Nouns

In this unit we use the types of nouns: common, proper, collective, concrete and abstract nouns. We also learn to use post modifiers that go after a noun, for example "the man in the blue shirt".

Nouns Written in Plural Form but Singular in Meaning

Some nouns look plural but are singular in meaning, and they take a singular verb, for example: "This news is good." The book gives news, scissors, glasses, tweezers, pants and jeans. Others of the same kind are shorts, mathematics, physics and economics.

Final list: news, scissors, glasses, tweezers, pants, jeans, shorts, mathematics, physics, economics.

Key Points

  • Nouns are of different types: common, proper, collective, concrete and abstract.
  • A post modifier comes after the noun it describes, as in "the man in the blue shirt".
  • Words like news, scissors, glasses, tweezers, pants and jeans are written in plural form but are singular in meaning, so they take a singular verb.

lessons.title: Grammar: Sentence Patterns SV and SVO
lessons.notes_html:
The SV Pattern

In the SV pattern there is a subject and an intransitive verb, and no object is needed. Each sentence is complete with only a subject and a verb.

  • The baby sleeps.
  • Birds fly.
  • She runs.

The SVO Pattern

In the SVO pattern there is a subject, a transitive verb and an object. In each sentence the verb passes its action to an object.

  • The boy hurled stones.
  • Sana dropped her mobile.
  • My mother buys a cake.

Key Points

  • SV = subject + verb. The verb is intransitive, so the sentence needs no object.
  • SVO = subject + verb + object. The verb is transitive and passes its action to the object.

lessons.title: Writing: A Paragraph about a Proud Moment
lessons.notes_html:
The Topic Sentence and Supporting Details

The writing lesson of this unit teaches us to write a paragraph of 9–10 lines about a proud moment in life. First we write the topic sentence, then we use supporting details to make it interesting, and we punctuate and capitalise the text properly. The unit's punctuation lesson is about capitalisation and full stops: a sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

A Model Paragraph

My proudest moment came on the day my school announced the annual examination result. I had worked hard all year, and my teachers had always encouraged me to keep trying. When my name was called first in the class, my heart filled with joy and my eyes filled with tears. My parents smiled with pride, and my friends clapped loudly for me. My teacher shook my hand and said that hard work always brings success. That day taught me that patience, honesty and regular study never go waste. I still remember that moment whenever I feel tired of studying, and it gives me fresh courage to work harder.

Key Points

  • Begin the paragraph with a clear topic sentence that tells what the paragraph is about.
  • Add supporting details in order to make the paragraph interesting.
  • Punctuate and capitalise properly: capital letters begin sentences, and full stops end them.

lessons.title: Reading: Eid ul Fitr
lessons.notes_html:
The Text in Short

Eid-ul-Fitr is celebrated at the start of Shawwal, the 10th month of the Islamic calendar, after the holy month of Ramadan ends. The celebrations start after the announcement of the Eid crescent, and the night before Eid is known as Chand Raat.

Another key element of Eid celebrations is to give fitrana — an obligatory payment to the poor and less fortunate families — prior to Eid namaz. It is charity which helps others to enjoy festivities as well. This way Muslims teach their children to help the needy and deserving as much as possible.

After Eid Salat, Muslims exchange Eid greetings. Kids get 'Eidi' from their elders in the form of new currency notes or other gifts.

Eid ul Fitr is also celebrated to show gratitude to Allah for His help and strength throughout the month, when He ensured that the Muslims accomplished their sacred duties during Ramadan. The Holy Quran was revealed to Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ in Ramadan.

The Eid festival is a national holiday in all Muslim countries. Eid is the time to forgive others by inviting or visiting them.

My Eid Day

On Eid day, I wake up early, wear my new clothes and go with my father to the masjid for Salat ul Eid. After the prayer, we hug our relatives and friends and wish them Eid Mubarak. At home, my mother serves sweet dishes, and my elders give me Eidi in the form of new currency notes or other gifts. In the evening, we visit our relatives, share food with our neighbours and enjoy the whole day with happiness and love.

Why I Like Eid

Eid-ul-Fitr comes after the holy month of Ramadan and brings happiness to every Muslim home. On Eid day we wear new clothes, offer Salat ul Eid, meet our relatives and enjoy sweet dishes together. Eid teaches us to share our happiness with the poor and to forgive others. The children in the unit's picture are celebrating Eid-ul-Fitr: they are hugging each other outside the masjid in new clothes, which is the traditional Eid greeting after Salat ul Eid, and the picture shows the joy and togetherness of Eid day.

Food on Eid-ul-Fitr

On Eid-ul-Fitr, families offer special Eid food and desserts, such as sweet made with vermicelli and milk, kheer and other local desserts. It is a tradition to wear new clothes on Eid day and to eat these special sweet dishes together with family and guests.

Junk Food on the Two Eids — A Discussion

The intake of junk food does increase on the two Eids, because guests are served cold drinks, fried snacks and sweets at every house. To avoid junk food, we should serve fresh fruit, homemade sweets and traditional dishes instead of packet food and fizzy drinks. We should also eat in small portions, drink water and share healthy food with our guests. In this way, we can enjoy Eid fully without harming our health.

The unit's dialogue shows a speaking situation at home: Usman brings all the things from the market for Eid day, but he forgets the milk and rice, which are the main ingredients for the Kheer his mother has to make, because he did not cross-check the things with her shopping list. His mother sends him again and tells him to be careful and not to forget anything this time.

Word Meanings

  • commemorates — honours. Eid-ul-Fitr commemorates the end of the holy month of Ramadan, and it honours the completion of fasting and the sacred duties performed during Ramadan.
  • audible — able to be heard. The voice of the Imam was clearly audible in the whole masjid during the Eid sermon, so every person in the congregation could hear it.
  • congregation — flock. A large congregation gathered in the masjid and in open places to offer Salat ul Eid together on the morning of Eid.
  • accomplishment — achievement. Completing the fasts of Ramadan is a great accomplishment, and Eid-ul-Fitr is the celebration of that achievement.
  • gratitude — thankfulness. Eid-ul-Fitr is celebrated to show gratitude to Allah for His help and strength throughout the month of Ramadan.
  • desserts — sweets. On Eid day, families eat special Eid desserts like sweet made with vermicelli and milk, kheer and other local desserts.

Key Points

  • Muslims celebrate Eid-ul-Fitr at the start of Shawwal, the 10th month of the Islamic calendar, after Ramadan ends.
  • Fitrana is an obligatory payment to the poor and less fortunate families, given prior to Eid namaz, so that the poor can also enjoy the festivities of Eid.
  • The purpose of Eid-ul-Fitr is to celebrate the completion of Ramadan and to show gratitude to Allah for His help and strength throughout the month. It is a time to forgive others, to help the poor through fitrana, and to bring peace and harmony among Muslims. Eid is also a national holiday in all Muslim countries, and it reminds Muslims of their sacred duties and of the revelation of the Holy Quran in Ramadan.
  • On Eid day, children receive Eidi from their elders, and everyone wears new clothes and shares sweet dishes with family, relatives and neighbours.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: Homographs
lessons.notes_html:
What Are Homographs?

Homographs are words that have the same spelling but different meanings, and sometimes they have different pronunciation as well. In this lesson we make two sentences from each word in a pair, one for each meaning.

The Book's Example Table

HomographsMeaningsExamples
resignto quitI am going to resign from the job.
resignto sign againCan you please resign the papers.
windto finishWind up your work.
windairThe cool wind blows.
leadto headI am going to lead this team.
leada type of matterThe lead of my pencil is broken.

Homographs in Sentences

  • bass (a fish): We caught a bass in the lake yesterday. bass (low sound): The singer sang in a deep bass voice that everyone could hear clearly.
  • minute (a very small thing): The minute details of the drawing showed the artist's great skill. minute (sixty seconds): Please wait a minute; I will come back soon.
  • firm (a company): My father works in a firm that builds houses. firm (strong and steady): Hold the rope with a firm grip so that it does not slip.
  • tear (a drop from the eye): A tear rolled down her cheek when she heard the sad news. tear (to rip): Be careful not to tear the paper while you open the parcel.
  • watch (a timepiece): My grandfather gave me a beautiful watch on my birthday. watch (to look at): We will watch the Eid programme on television tonight.

Key Points

  • Homographs have the same spelling but different meanings; the meaning is known from the sentence.
  • Some homographs also change their pronunciation with the meaning, like bass, minute and lead.

mcqs.q: What are homographs?
options: Words that sound the same but are spelled differently
Words that have the same spelling but different meanings
Two words joined into one word
Words that mean exactly the same
mcqs.why: The lesson defines homographs as words that have the same spelling but different meanings, and sometimes different pronunciation as well.

mcqs.q: In the sentence 'Wind up your work', the word 'wind' means:

lessons.title: Grammar: Gender Nouns
lessons.notes_html:
The Four Genders

Nouns are sorted under their respective headings according to gender. Masculine gender represents males, feminine gender represents females, common gender nouns are used for both males and females, and neuter gender nouns refer to inanimate objects.

GenderNouns
Masculine Genderlion, waiter, farmer
Feminine Genderhen, nurse
Common Gendercousin
Neuter Gendercastle, feather
  • Masculine: lion, waiter and farmer are masculine, because they represent males.
  • Feminine: hen and nurse (shown as a female nurse in the book) are feminine, because they represent females.
  • Common: cousin can be a boy or a girl, so it is common gender.
  • Neuter: castle and feather are inanimate objects, so they are neuter gender.

Key Points

  • There are four genders of nouns: masculine, feminine, common and neuter.
  • Common gender nouns, like cousin, are used for both males and females; neuter gender nouns name things without life.

lessons.title: Grammar: Pronouns — Personal, Interrogative and Demonstrative
lessons.notes_html:
Personal Pronouns

Personal pronouns are used in three forms: subjective pronouns (I, we, you, he, she), objective pronouns (me, us, you, him, her) and possessive pronouns (mine, ours, yours, his, hers).

  • Subjective: I am not feeling well today. We are going on a picnic. She is making tea.
  • Objective: Ali gave me a very cute pet cat. Who is going with us? Mother helped her in making tea.
  • Possessive: This pair of shoes is mine. This picnic basket is ours. These notebooks are not his; they are hers.

Interrogative Pronouns

Interrogative pronouns are used to ask questions. Each of these sentences asks a question and ends with a question mark.

  • How do you celebrate Eid-ul-Fitr with your family?
  • When will you go to the masjid for Salat ul Eid?
  • Whom did you meet first on Eid morning?
  • What is your favourite Eid dish?
  • Why do Muslims give fitrana before Eid namaz?

Demonstrative Pronouns

Demonstrative pronouns are this, that, these and those. This and these point to things close to the speaker, while that and those point to things far from the speaker.

  • Look at this!
  • That looks like a fox.
  • There are many flowers. Do you like these?
  • Maha wears her mother's clothes. She looks odd in those.
  • This is my new dress for Eid.
  • That is the masjid where we offer Salat ul Eid.
  • These are the sweets my mother made for Eid.
  • Those children are hugging each other after the Eid prayer.

Subject–Verb–Adjective (SVA)

In an SVA sentence, the subject comes first, the verb second, and the adjective third, describing the subject.

  • She was sick. — Subject: She. Verb: was. Adjective: sick.
  • He ran fast. — Subject: He. Verb: ran. Adjective/adverb: fast, which describes how he ran.
  • He is intelligent. — Subject: He. Verb: is. Adjective: intelligent, which describes the subject He.
  • The truck is big. — Subject: The truck. Verb: is. Adjective: big, which describes the truck.
  • The workers are lazy. — Subject: The workers. Verb: are. Adjective: lazy, which describes the workers.

Key Points

  • Personal pronouns change their form: subjective (I, we, he, she), objective (me, us, him, her) and possessive (mine, ours, his, hers).
  • Interrogative pronouns — how, when, whom, what, why — begin question sentences, which end with a question mark.
  • This and these point to near things; that and those point to far things.
  • In the SVA pattern, the adjective comes after the verb and describes the subject.

lessons.title: Grammar: Tenses and Will/Shall
lessons.notes_html:
Present Simple — Choosing the Correct Form

  • I play football every Saturday. The subject I takes the present form play without s or es.
  • Do they listen to rap music? The subject they is plural, so Do is used, not Does.
  • Majid doesn't set the table. Majid is a singular subject, so does + not (doesn't) is used.
  • We sometimes go to the park. The subject We takes the present form go without s.
  • I don't watch television after nine p.m. The subject I takes do + not (don't), as the book states that Do is used for I and you.
  • They often visit their grandparents on the weekends. The plural subject They takes visit, not visits.
  • Does she like mangoes? The singular subject she takes Does.
  • My rabbit always eats very fast. The singular subject My rabbit takes eats with s.
  • Does Amana travel abroad every year? Amana is a singular subject, so Does is used.
  • Saad doesn't play computer games on Saturdays. Saad is a singular subject, so doesn't is used.

Simple Past Tense

  • The show began at 10:30.
  • The children threw the ball.
  • We bought a new pair of shoes last Friday.
  • Amana came from Multan.
  • They drank two liters of water yesterday.

Will and Shall

  • I shall wear a sweater next week.
  • He will buy a new shirt next month.
  • When will you go to Canada again?
  • We shall play football next Monday.
  • They will visit their parents next week.

Key Points

  • Singular subjects take the verb with s/es and Does/doesn't; plural subjects and I/you take the base verb and Do/don't.
  • The simple past tense tells about finished actions: began, threw, bought, came, drank.
  • Will and shall are used for actions of the future time.

mcqs.why: Majid is a singular subject, so does + not (doesn't) is used, as the lesson explains.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct word: '______ she like mangoes?'
mcqs.why: The lesson states that the singular subject 'she' takes Does in a present simple question.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct form: 'My rabbit always ______ very fast.'
mcqs.why: The singular subject 'My rabbit' takes the verb with s, so the correct form is 'eats'.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct form: 'They often ______ their grandparents on the weekends.'
mcqs.why: The lesson explains that the plural subject 'They' takes the base form 'visit', not 'visits'.

lessons.title: Punctuation: The Exclamation Mark
lessons.notes_html:
Exclamatory Sentences

An exclamation mark is used with a sentence showing strong feeling, and the sentence begins with a capital letter. Words like Wow, Hurray, Alas, Yay and Well-done show strong feelings of surprise, joy, sorrow, happiness and praise.

  • Wow! Your birthday gift is beautiful. — The exclamation mark is used with the sentence showing strong feeling, Wow.
  • Hurray! I scored full marks in my math test. — Hurray shows strong joy, so it takes an exclamation mark.
  • Alas! I lost my purse. — Alas shows strong sorrow, so it takes an exclamation mark.
  • Yay! We made it. — Yay shows strong happiness, so it takes an exclamation mark.
  • Well-done! What a great job. — Well-done shows praise and strong feeling, so it takes an exclamation mark.

Key Points

  • Use an exclamation mark after words and sentences that show strong feeling.
  • After the exclamation mark, the next sentence begins with a capital letter.

lessons.title: Writing: A Narrative Paragraph
lessons.notes_html:
Planning, Drafting and Reviewing

The writing lesson of this unit teaches us to write a narrative paragraph about a time when we met our best friend for the very first time, following the planning, drafting and reviewing guidelines of the book.

Planning. The planning questions are: What is the topic? Who are the characters? What is the setting (when/where)? Who is the main protagonist? What is the main idea, event and problem of the story? For this paragraph: the topic is the first meeting with my best friend; the characters are I and my best friend Ahmed; the setting is my classroom on the first day of class six; the main protagonist is I, the narrator, who meets his best friend; the main idea and event is that a shy new student finds a kind classmate and their friendship begins, and the problem is the narrator's nervousness on the first day, which ends when Ahmed speaks to him kindly.

Drafting. Write the heading on top of the page, organise the events in the right order, use simple past tense and vocabulary that shows the characters' feelings.

Reviewing. Check that the writing contains the heading, characters, setting, key details, main idea and ending, and proofread the final draft for errors.

A Model Narrative Paragraph

I still remember the day I met my best friend for the very first time. It was my first day in class six, and I sat alone on a bench near the window, feeling shy and nervous. A boy named Ahmed came and sat beside me, smiled warmly and asked my name. We talked about our favourite games, and soon we discovered that we both loved cricket and reading storybooks. From that day, we sat together in class, played together in the ground and helped each other in our studies. That first meeting changed my school life completely, because I found a true friend who stands by me in happiness and in difficulty. I will always remember that day with joy and gratitude.

Key Points

  • A narrative paragraph tells a story in the simple past tense, with events in the right order.
  • Plan first: topic, characters, setting, main protagonist, main idea, event and problem.
  • Review at the end: heading, characters, setting, key details, main idea and ending — then proofread for errors.
